overview: Data sharing lets one organization grant another live, read-only access to its warehouse data without copying, moving, or ETL-ing it -- the consumer queries the provider's data in place using their own compute.

A data marketplace is a discovery and distribution layer built on top of sharing: providers list datasets (free, public, or paid) and consumers find, subscribe to, and instantly query them, turning data into a productized, monetizable asset.

Each major warehouse implements this natively: Snowflake Secure Data Sharing and the Snowflake Marketplace, BigQuery data sharing via Analytics Hub (listings and exchanges), and Amazon Redshift data sharing (datashares) plus AWS Data Exchange for third-party data.
learningObjectives: Explain zero-copy, in-place data sharing and why it eliminates the traditional extract-transfer-load-and-reconcile pipeline between organizations.
Describe how Snowflake shares, BigQuery Analytics Hub listings, and Redshift datashares grant governed access and how each bills provider vs consumer compute.
Design a governed share: expose only specific objects via secure views/row filters, control access, and revoke cleanly.
Understand marketplaces for discovery and monetization, including listings, subscriptions, and the difference between free/public and paid/private data products.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Data sharing is a warehouse capability that grants a consumer account governed, read-only, live access to a defined set of a provider's database objects (tables, views, and functions) without physically copying the data, such that the consumer queries the provider's committed data in place using the consumer's own compute; a data marketplace layers discovery, listing, subscription, and (optionally) monetization on top of that sharing primitive.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Traditionally, sharing data meant exporting it to files, transferring them, and re-loading them into another system -- slow, stale, and expensive, with two copies to keep in sync. Modern warehouse sharing is like giving someone a library card to your shelves instead of photocopying every book: they read your live data directly, always current, with no copy made. A marketplace is the library catalog where anyone can discover and 'check out' (subscribe to) datasets, some free and some paid.
coreConcept.historicalContext: For decades, cross-organization data exchange meant FTP files, SFTP drops, or nightly extracts loaded into the recipient's system, producing stale duplicates and reconciliation nightmares. Snowflake pioneered zero-copy Secure Data Sharing in 2018 by exploiting its storage-compute separation -- the provider grants metadata references, the consumer queries with their own compute over the same immutable storage -- and launched the Snowflake Data Marketplace (now Marketplace) in 2019. BigQuery followed with Analytics Hub (GA 2023) built on authorized/shared datasets, and Redshift introduced datashares (2021) for cross-cluster and cross-account sharing, complemented by AWS Data Exchange. Sharing shifted from a batch data-movement problem to a governance-and-access-control problem.

whyItMatters.business: Sharing turns data into a distributable, monetizable product: companies sell curated datasets on marketplaces, and partners exchange data instantly instead of over weeks. It also collapses partner-onboarding time from months of pipeline building to minutes of granting access.
whyItMatters.engineering: Zero-copy sharing eliminates entire classes of brittle inter-company ETL, file transfers, and reconciliation jobs; engineers grant governed access once instead of maintaining perpetual export/import pipelines.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because consumers bring their own compute and no data is copied, one provider can serve thousands of consumers over the same storage without scaling data movement; adding a consumer is a metadata operation.
whyItMatters.cost: No duplicate storage, no egress-heavy transfers, and no ETL compute for sharing; the provider pays only to store data once and the consumer pays only for the compute they use to query it.
whyItMatters.reliability: Consumers always see the provider's live, committed data with no synchronization lag or drift, removing the stale-copy failures endemic to file-based exchange, and access can be revoked instantly and completely.

coreComponents.name: Provider
coreComponents.definition: The account that owns the source data and creates a share/listing/datashare defining exactly which objects are exposed and to whom.
coreComponents.purpose: To publish governed, read-only access to selected data while retaining full ownership and control.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Curate the objects to expose (often via secure views), add them to a share, grant it to specific consumers or list it on a marketplace, and revoke access when needed.
coreComponents.examples: A weather-data company creating a Snowflake share of its forecast tables; a marketing firm publishing a BigQuery Analytics Hub listing.

coreComponents.name: Consumer
coreComponents.definition: The account that is granted access and queries the shared objects in place using its own compute, seeing the provider's live data.
coreComponents.purpose: To use fresh external data immediately without building ingestion pipelines or storing a copy.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Mount/import the share (as a read-only database/dataset), query it with the consumer's own warehouse/slots, and pay for its own query compute.
coreComponents.examples: A retailer subscribing to a demographics dataset on the Snowflake Marketplace; an analyst querying an Analytics Hub linked dataset.

coreComponents.name: Share / Listing / Datashare
coreComponents.definition: The named object that packages the exposed database objects and the access grant: a Snowflake SHARE, a BigQuery Analytics Hub LISTING (in an exchange), or a Redshift DATASHARE.
coreComponents.purpose: To define the unit of sharing -- what is exposed, who can access it, and (on a marketplace) how it is discovered and priced.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Enumerate the shared schemas/tables/views/functions, bind them to grantees or a marketplace listing, and serve as the revocation handle.
coreComponents.examples: CREATE SHARE weather_share; an Analytics Hub listing 'Global Weather'; CREATE DATASHARE sales_share.

coreComponents.name: Secure View / Row & Column Governance Layer
coreComponents.definition: Views and policies that restrict what the consumer can see -- hiding sensitive columns, filtering rows per consumer, and preventing exposure of the underlying object definitions.
coreComponents.purpose: To share only the intended slice of data safely, enforcing least-privilege at the share boundary.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Project only allowed columns, apply row filters (e.g., per-consumer or region), and mask or exclude sensitive fields before data leaves the provider.
coreComponents.examples: A Snowflake secure view exposing aggregated sales without customer PII; a BigQuery authorized view filtered per subscriber.

coreComponents.name: Marketplace / Exchange
coreComponents.definition: The catalog and distribution layer where providers publish listings and consumers discover, subscribe to, and instantly query data products (free, public, or paid).
coreComponents.purpose: To make sharing a productized, discoverable, and monetizable channel rather than a bilateral grant.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Host listings with metadata and terms, manage subscriptions and (for paid) billing, and provision the underlying share/datashare on subscription.
coreComponents.examples: Snowflake Marketplace, BigQuery Analytics Hub public exchanges, AWS Data Exchange for third-party data on Redshift.

internalWorking: The provider curates the objects to expose -- typically through secure views that project only allowed columns and apply row filters -- so the share exposes a governed slice, not raw base tables.

The provider creates a share/listing/datashare, adds those objects, and grants it to named consumer accounts or publishes it to a marketplace/exchange; internally this records metadata pointers to the provider's storage, not a data copy.
The consumer imports the share as a read-only database/dataset (or subscribes on the marketplace, which auto-provisions the mount); no bytes are transferred, only access metadata.

When the consumer runs a query, it executes on the consumer's own compute against the provider's immutable storage layer, so the consumer always reads the provider's latest committed data with no synchronization step.

Access is fully governed and revocable: the provider can alter the share's object set, tighten the secure views/policies, or drop the grant, and the change takes effect immediately because there is no distributed copy to invalidate.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Provider curates objects (secure views + row/column policies) -> creates Share/Listing/Datashare -> grants to consumer accounts OR publishes to Marketplace/Exchange -> consumer subscribes/imports as read-only DB/dataset (metadata only, zero copy) -> consumer queries in place with own compute -> reads provider's live committed data -> provider can alter/revoke instantly
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A weather-data provider builds secure views over its raw forecast tables that expose only region, date, and forecast columns (no proprietary model internals).
2. The provider runs CREATE SHARE weather_share, adds the secure views, and either GRANTs it to a specific retailer's account or publishes it as a Marketplace listing.
3. The retailer discovers the listing, subscribes, and Snowflake auto-creates a read-only database in their account pointing at the provider's data -- no bytes copied, done in seconds.
4. The retailer's analysts query the shared views using the retailer's own warehouse; the query runs on the retailer's compute over the provider's storage.
5. When the provider publishes tomorrow's forecast, the retailer's next query immediately sees it -- always live, no reload.
6. If the contract ends, the provider revokes the share; the retailer instantly loses access with no orphaned copies left behind.

keyTerminology.meaning: Granting access to data via metadata references so the consumer queries the provider's storage directly, with no physical copy or transfer.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the core innovation: it removes duplicate storage, egress, ETL, and staleness, and makes onboarding a consumer a metadata operation.

keyTerminology.meaning: A view whose definition is hidden from consumers and which projects/filters data so only intended columns and rows are exposed through a share.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the primary governance mechanism for sharing: it lets you expose a safe slice (e.g., aggregates without PII) rather than raw tables.

keyTerminology.meaning: A named container of database objects a Redshift producer cluster/namespace shares with consumer clusters/namespaces, across clusters and accounts.
keyTerminology.importance: It is Redshift's sharing primitive, enabling live cross-cluster and cross-account access without unloading and reloading data.

keyTerminology.meaning: A published, discoverable data product (listing) grouped in a private or public exchange; subscribing creates a linked dataset in the consumer's project.
keyTerminology.importance: It is BigQuery's marketplace/exchange layer for governed, discoverable sharing across projects and organizations.

keyTerminology.meaning: A catalog entry describing a shared dataset (free, public, or paid) with metadata and terms that consumers can discover and subscribe to.
keyTerminology.importance: It turns bilateral sharing into a scalable, monetizable distribution channel with discovery and billing.

keyTerminology.meaning: A provider-managed account created for a consumer who is not themselves a Snowflake customer, so they can query shared data.
keyTerminology.importance: It lets providers share with non-Snowflake consumers while the provider pays for the reader's compute.

importantConcepts.explanation: Traditional exchange copies data (export -> transfer -> load), creating a second, immediately-stale copy that must be reconciled and re-shipped on every update, incurring storage, egress, and ETL cost. Zero-copy sharing instead grants a live metadata reference: the consumer reads the provider's single stored copy in place. There is nothing to synchronize, no duplicate storage, and updates are visible instantly. This inverts the problem from 'move data reliably' to 'govern access precisely'.

importantConcepts.concept: Who pays for compute (provider vs consumer)
importantConcepts.explanation: In standard sharing the consumer brings and pays for their own compute to query the provider's data, and the provider pays only to store the data once -- an elegant cost split. The exception is when the provider serves non-customers via a Snowflake reader account (provider pays that compute) or a Marketplace provider chooses to subsidize. Understanding this split is essential for pricing a data product and for consumers budgeting query cost on shared data.

Sharing raw base tables is dangerous; the disciplined pattern is to expose only secure views with column projection, row-level filters (often per consumer), and masking of sensitive fields, so the share surface is the minimum necessary. Because the consumer queries live, any policy tightening or revocation takes effect immediately. Governance -- not data movement -- is the hard part of sharing, and it is where PII/compliance risk lives.

A marketplace layers discovery, subscription, and billing on the sharing primitive so data becomes a product. Listings can be free/public (open data, samples) or paid/private (commercial datasets, per-consumer terms). This creates a two-sided market: providers monetize curated data and reach many consumers with one listing, while consumers get instantly-queryable external data without pipelines. The economics work because zero-copy makes serving each new consumer nearly free for the provider.

Sharing is trivially instant within the same region/cloud because it is pure metadata. Across regions or clouds, the platform must replicate the data to the target region first (incurring storage and transfer cost and a replication lag), after which local consumers get zero-copy access. Providers serving a global audience therefore replicate their share to each region rather than sharing across the wire on every query -- a key design and cost consideration.

variationsAndTypes: **Snowflake direct share:** Provider grants a SHARE to specific consumer accounts for private, bilateral sharing.
**Snowflake Marketplace listing:** Public or private listings (free or paid) discoverable by any Snowflake account, auto-provisioning a read-only database on subscription.
**Snowflake reader account:** Provider-managed account so non-Snowflake consumers can query shared data (provider pays compute).
**BigQuery Analytics Hub listing:** Published data product in a private or public exchange; subscribing creates a linked (read-only) dataset in the consumer's project.
**Redshift datashare (intra-account):** Live sharing between clusters/namespaces in one account (e.g., producer ETL cluster to consumer BI cluster).
**Redshift datashare (cross-account) + AWS Data Exchange:** Governed cross-account sharing and a marketplace for licensed third-party data.
**Cross-region/cross-cloud replicated share:** Data replicated to the target region/cloud first, then shared zero-copy locally.
advantages: **No copying or ETL:** Eliminates export/transfer/load pipelines and duplicate storage between organizations.
**Always live:** Consumers see the provider's latest committed data with zero synchronization lag.
**Instant onboarding & revocation:** Granting or removing access is a metadata operation done in seconds.
**Clean cost split:** Provider stores once; consumer pays for its own query compute.
**Monetization & discovery:** Marketplaces turn data into a discoverable, sellable product served to many consumers from one copy.
disadvantages: **Governance burden shifts to sharing:** Exposing the wrong columns/rows is a data-leak risk; requires disciplined secure views and policies.
**Platform lock-in for native zero-copy:** Native sharing generally works within the same platform (Snowflake-to-Snowflake, etc.); cross-platform sharing needs replication or connectors.
**Cross-region cost/lag:** Serving other regions requires replication, adding storage, transfer cost, and lag.
**Consumer compute cost surprises:** Consumers querying huge shared datasets can incur large compute bills unless bounded.
**Limited transformation:** Consumers get read-only access; they cannot modify shared objects, so heavy reshaping still needs local copies.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use native sharing when provider and consumer are on the same platform, data must stay live, and you want to avoid pipelines -- ideal for partner data exchange, internal cross-team/BU sharing, and monetizing datasets on a marketplace.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid relying on native sharing when consumers are on a different platform (use replication/export or a neutral format), when consumers must heavily transform or persist the data (copy locally), or when strict data-residency forbids replication to the consumer's region.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Traditional data exchange is like mailing photocopies of a report to every partner: expensive to print and ship, instantly out of date, and you can never fully recall a copy. Zero-copy sharing is like giving partners live read-only access to a shared Google Doc: they always see the current version, no copies exist, and you can revoke access with one click. A marketplace is the shared drive's public folder where anyone can browse and request access to published documents, some free and some paid.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Data sharing copies the data into the consumer's account.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Native sharing is zero-copy: the consumer queries the provider's storage in place via metadata references. No bytes are duplicated (except when crossing regions, which requires replication).

commonMisconceptions.myth: The provider pays for the consumer's queries.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In standard sharing the consumer brings and pays for their own compute; the provider pays only to store the data once. The exception is Snowflake reader accounts, where the provider pays for the non-customer consumer's compute.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Once shared, you cannot control or take back the data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Access is fully governed and instantly revocable; because it is live metadata access, tightening a secure view or dropping the share takes effect immediately with no orphaned copies -- far more controllable than file exports.

productionConsiderations.scalability: One provider serves many consumers over a single stored copy; adding a consumer is a metadata grant, so sharing scales with consumers without scaling data movement. For global audiences, replicate the share per region.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Consumers always read live committed data, removing stale-copy failures; ensure secure views and policies are correct so the exposed slice is stable across provider schema changes.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because access is metadata, there is no fragile transfer pipeline to fail; design shares over stable secure views so provider refactors do not break consumer queries.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track who is subscribed, which objects are exposed, consumer query patterns on shared data, and (for cross-region) replication lag and cost.
productionConsiderations.security: Expose only secure views with column projection and row filters; never share raw PII tables; audit share grants and marketplace listings; enforce least-privilege at the share boundary.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoid unnecessary cross-region replication; for monetized shares model consumer compute; consumers should bound queries on large shared datasets with pruning/limits.
productionConsiderations.performance: Consumers query with their own compute, so provide well-clustered/partitioned shared objects and secure views that prune efficiently to keep consumer query cost and latency low.

codeExamples.title: Snowflake: Create a Governed Secure Data Share
codeExamples.overview: Builds a secure view exposing only safe columns/rows, packages it in a share, grants it to a consumer account, and shows how the consumer imports and queries it.
codeExamples.breakdown: The secure view exposes only aggregated, non-PII columns -- governance at the share boundary. The share is granted USAGE on the database/schema and SELECT on the view only, so nothing else is visible. Adding the consumer's account locator grants access; the consumer mounts it as a read-only database and queries live data with their own warehouse. REMOVE ACCOUNTS revokes instantly, zero-copy, with no orphaned data.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Share created and granted; consumer's CREATE DATABASE ... FROM SHARE succeeds in seconds (no data copied). The consumer query returns live per-region YTD sales. After REMOVE ACCOUNTS, the consumer's queries on shared_sales fail with an access error.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Sharing a raw base table instead of a secure view can leak PII and expose object definitions; forgetting USAGE grants on the parent database/schema makes the view invisible; sharing across regions silently fails until you replicate the data first.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always share secure views, never raw tables; keep the view stable so provider refactors do not break consumers; cluster/partition the underlying data so consumer queries prune; for global consumers replicate the database to their region and share the replica.

codeExamples.title: BigQuery Analytics Hub: Publish and Subscribe to a Listing
codeExamples.overview: Creates a data exchange and a listing over an authorized view, then subscribes from a consumer project to get a read-only linked dataset.
codeExamples.code:
# PROVIDER: create an exchange to hold listings
bq mk --data_exchange --location=US \
  --display_name="Partner Data Exchange" partner_exchange

# Create a listing that shares a governed (authorized-view) dataset
bq mk --listing --location=US \
  --data_exchange=partner_exchange \
  --display_name="Regional Sales (Governed)" \
  --source_dataset=my-provider-project:shared_sales_views \
  regional_sales_listing

# CONSUMER: subscribe -> creates a read-only linked dataset in the consumer project
bq mk --subscription --location=US \
  --listing=projects/my-provider-project/locations/US/dataExchanges/partner_exchange/listings/regional_sales_listing \
  --destination_dataset=my-consumer-project:linked_regional_sales

# CONSUMER: query the linked dataset like any local dataset (live, zero-copy)
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false \
  'SELECT region, SUM(total_sales) AS ytd FROM `my-consumer-project.linked_regional_sales.sales_by_region` GROUP BY region'
codeExamples.breakdown: The provider creates an exchange (a container) and a listing that publishes a governed dataset -- ideally one built from authorized views that project/filter safely. The consumer subscribes, which creates a read-only linked dataset in their project pointing at the provider's data (no copy). The consumer then queries it with their own slots exactly like a local dataset, always seeing live data.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Exchange and listing created; the consumer subscription creates linked_regional_sales; the query returns live per-region YTD totals computed on the consumer's compute. Removing the listing or subscription revokes access.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Publishing a raw dataset instead of authorized views can over-expose; cross-region listings require the source in the consumer's region; IAM on the exchange/listing must permit the intended subscribers or subscription fails.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Share authorized views for governance, keep exchanges private for partner-only data, use labels for discovery, and partition/cluster source tables so consumer queries prune and cost less.

codeExamples.title: Redshift: Create and Consume a Datashare
codeExamples.overview: A producer cluster creates a datashare, adds schema objects, grants it to a consumer namespace/account, and the consumer creates a database from it to query live.
codeExamples.breakdown: The producer defines a datashare, adds the schema and object (best practice: a view exposing only safe columns), and grants USAGE to a consumer namespace (intra-account) or another AWS account (cross-account). The consumer creates a local database FROM DATASHARE and queries it live with its own cluster/RPUs -- no unload/reload. SHOW DATASHARES and svv_datashare_objects audit what is exposed.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Datashare created and granted; the consumer's CREATE DATABASE FROM DATASHARE succeeds and the query returns live per-region totals. svv_datashare_objects lists the exposed schema/table.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Adding raw tables instead of governed views over-exposes; cross-account sharing requires the consumer to authorize/associate the datashare in the console; RA3 (managed storage) is required for datasharing; producer schema drops can break consumer queries.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Expose views rather than base tables, keep producer schemas stable, use RA3 nodes, and monitor svv_datashare_* views; for BI-vs-ETL isolation, share from a producer cluster to a separate consumer BI cluster.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A market-research firm wants to sell curated consumer-spending datasets to hundreds of retail clients. Historically it exported CSVs monthly and SFTP'd them to each client -- stale by weeks, expensive to maintain, and impossible to revoke. It wants a live, governed, monetizable data product with instant onboarding.
endToEndExample.inputData: A large Snowflake table of consumer transactions containing PII (names, card hashes) plus derived spend metrics by category and region. Clients must see only aggregated, de-identified spend, filtered to the categories they purchased.
endToEndExample.architecture: Snowflake provider account with secure views over the raw data, a Marketplace listing (paid, private offers per client), row-level filtering per subscriber, and per-region replicas for global clients.
processingSteps: 1. Build secure views that aggregate transactions to category/region spend and exclude all PII, plus a row-access policy limiting each client to the categories in their contract.
2. Create a share containing only those secure views (USAGE on db/schema, SELECT on views) so nothing raw is ever exposed.
3. Publish a Marketplace listing with rich metadata and terms; use private listings/offers so pricing and access are per-client.
4. Onboard a client by accepting them to the listing -- Snowflake auto-provisions a read-only database in their account in seconds, no pipeline.
5. For clients in other regions, replicate the provider database to those regions and list the regional replica so cross-region consumers get zero-copy local access.
6. Bill via the marketplace; monitor subscriptions, exposed objects, and per-region replication cost/lag.
endToEndExample.output: A live, governed, paid data product: each client queries de-identified, category-filtered spend directly, always current, onboarded in minutes and revocable instantly, with the firm monetizing via the marketplace.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track active subscriptions and per-client access, audit which objects the share exposes, watch consumer query patterns and any policy exceptions, and monitor cross-region replication lag and cost.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Row-access policies and secure views prevent leakage even if a view is misqueried; if a client contract ends, revoke the listing offer and access drops instantly; if a provider schema change would break consumers, it is caught because consumers query the stable secure views, not base tables.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Client onboarding drops from weeks of SFTP pipeline setup to minutes, data is always live instead of weeks stale, PII never leaves the provider thanks to secure views and row policies, access is instantly revocable, and the firm turns its data into a recurring-revenue marketplace product served to hundreds of clients from one stored copy.

industryUseCases.problem: Selling datasets via file exports was stale, costly, unrevocable, and slow to onboard clients.
industryUseCases.solution: Publish governed secure views as paid Marketplace/Analytics Hub listings with per-client row filtering and per-region replicas.
industryUseCases.benefits: Live data, minutes-not-weeks onboarding, instant revocation, no PII leakage, and a scalable monetization channel served from one copy.

industryUseCases.problem: Retailers and suppliers needed to exchange sales and inventory data but ran fragile nightly file pipelines that produced stale, reconciliation-heavy copies.
industryUseCases.solution: Bilateral zero-copy shares/datashares of governed views so each side queries the other's live data with their own compute.
industryUseCases.benefits: Eliminated inter-company ETL, always-current shared metrics, and instant access changes when partnerships evolve.

industryUseCases.problem: Business units copied each other's data via ETL, creating duplicates, drift, and governance gaps.
industryUseCases.solution: Internal shares/datashares/Analytics-Hub exchanges so each domain publishes governed products consumed live by other BUs.
industryUseCases.benefits: Single source of truth, no duplicate storage or drift, clear domain ownership, and governed self-service access across the organization.

productionDeepDive.scalability: A single stored copy serves unlimited consumers because access is metadata; onboarding scales as grants/subscriptions, not data movement. For global reach, replicate the share per region so each region's consumers get local zero-copy access rather than cross-region query latency.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: There is no fragile transfer pipeline to fail; the main risk is provider schema drift breaking consumer queries, mitigated by sharing stable secure views and versioning them. Cross-region shares depend on replication health, which must be monitored.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Consumers depend on the provider's storage availability; the managed platform replicates storage durably. For HA across regions/clouds, maintain replicated shares so a regional outage does not cut off consumers who can point at another replica.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Share/listing/datashare definitions and secure-view/policy logic must be codified as infrastructure-as-code so they can be recreated after a DR rebuild; otherwise a restored account has data but no shares. Replicas double as DR copies for cross-region consumers.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Because consumers use their own compute, provide well-clustered/partitioned underlying tables and secure views that prune, so consumer queries scan minimally; avoid exposing views that force full scans, which inflate consumer cost and latency.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Avoid unnecessary cross-region replication (it duplicates storage and adds transfer cost); for reader accounts remember the provider pays compute; consumers should bound queries on large shared datasets with filters/limits; monetized providers must model consumer compute economics.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: This is the crux of sharing: expose only secure/authorized views with column projection and per-consumer row filters, never raw PII tables; audit every grant and listing; use private listings/offers for sensitive commercial data; and treat share configuration as high-privilege, reviewed change.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track active subscriptions/grants, the exact objects each share exposes (svv_datashare_objects, share metadata), consumer query activity, policy exceptions, and cross-region replication lag and cost; alert on unexpected new grants or exposed objects.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that secure views expose exactly the intended columns/rows (no PII leakage) via automated checks, and that they remain correct after provider schema changes; ensure aggregates in shared views reconcile with source truth.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log all share/listing/datashare grants, revocations, and consumer subscriptions; alert on any change to a share's exposed object set, new consumer additions, and cross-region replication failures so leakage or breakage is caught immediately.

recommendedPractices: **Always share secure/authorized views, never raw base tables,** so column projection and row filters govern exactly what leaves the provider.
**Apply per-consumer row-level policies** so each subscriber sees only its entitled slice of a shared object.
**Onboard and revoke via metadata grants/subscriptions,** exploiting instant zero-copy access changes instead of file pipelines.
**Replicate shares per region for global consumers** rather than serving cross-region queries over the wire.
**Audit every grant, listing, and exposed object** and treat share configuration as high-privilege change.
engineeringStandards: No share may expose a raw table containing PII; all shares expose reviewed secure/authorized views.
Share, listing, and datashare definitions plus their governing policies are version-controlled infrastructure-as-code.
Every consumer grant/subscription is logged and periodically re-reviewed against active contracts.
Cross-region sharing requires an explicit replication and cost review before publishing.
designRecommendations: Design shared secure views to be stable and forward-compatible so provider schema refactors do not break consumers.
Cluster/partition the underlying data and write pruning-friendly views so consumers' own-compute queries stay cheap and fast.
Prefer private listings/offers for commercial or sensitive data; reserve public listings for open/sample data.
Use reader accounts (Snowflake) only when consumers are non-customers, and budget for the provider-paid compute.
namingConventions: Name shares/listings/datashares by dataset and audience (e.g., sales_share, regional_sales_listing).
Name shared secure views to signal they are governed exposure surfaces (e.g., *_shared or *_secure).
Tag/label listings with domain and sensitivity for discovery and access control.
documentationStandards: Document each share's exposed objects, the governance (columns/rows filtered), and the entitled consumers/terms.
Record cross-region replication topology and its cost for every globally-shared dataset.
Maintain a data-product catalog entry per listing with owner, freshness, and contact.
testingStrategies: Test that secure/authorized views expose exactly the intended columns/rows and leak no PII, as an automated check.
Verify revocation truly cuts consumer access immediately and leaves no orphaned copies.
Test consumer queries after provider schema changes to confirm stable views did not break.
For cross-region shares, validate replication completeness and lag before consumers rely on the replica.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sharing raw base tables instead of secure/authorized views.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the quickest way to expose data and skips building a governance layer.
commonMistakes.impact: PII and proprietary columns leak to consumers, and object definitions are exposed -- a serious data-protection incident.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Expose only secure/authorized views with column projection and per-consumer row filters; never add raw PII tables to a share.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming sharing works across regions/clouds automatically.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: In-region sharing is instant metadata, so teams expect the same across regions.
commonMistakes.impact: Cross-region shares silently fail or perform poorly until the data is replicated to the target region.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Replicate the shared database/dataset to the consumer's region first, then share the local replica for zero-copy access.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting provider schema changes break consumer queries.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Providers refactor base tables without realizing consumers query them (directly or via unstable views).
commonMistakes.impact: Consumers' live queries suddenly fail, damaging the data-product relationship.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Share stable, versioned secure views as the contract surface, and change base tables behind them without altering the exposed shape.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring who pays for compute in a shared/reader arrangement.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams focus on storage and forget the query-compute split, especially with reader accounts.
commonMistakes.impact: Providers get surprise compute bills from reader-account consumers, or consumers get surprise bills querying huge shared datasets.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Confirm the compute-payer model (consumer pays normally; provider pays for reader accounts), and bound consumer queries with pruning-friendly views and limits.

comparisonSection.explanation: A Snowflake share grants named consumer accounts (or a Marketplace listing) read-only access, mounted as a database; the consumer queries live data zero-copy. A BigQuery Analytics Hub listing lives in an exchange, and subscribing creates a read-only linked dataset in the consumer's project. Both are zero-copy and governed; the difference is the object model (share/database vs listing/linked-dataset).

File-based exchange copies data, producing stale duplicates that must be reconciled and re-shipped on every update, with storage and egress cost and no clean revocation. Native sharing grants live metadata access to a single stored copy: always current, no duplicate storage, instant onboarding and revocation. The trade-off is native sharing usually requires both parties on the same platform.

In a standard share the consumer brings and pays for their own warehouse/slots; the provider pays only to store the data once -- ideal economics for a marketplace. A reader account lets a provider serve a non-Snowflake consumer, but then the provider pays for that consumer's query compute, so it must be budgeted and bounded.

Exposing secure/authorized views with column projection and per-consumer row filters shares only the intended, de-identified slice and hides object internals -- the safe pattern. Exposing raw tables leaks PII and definitions and couples consumers to your physical schema. Governance at the share boundary, not data movement, is the real work of sharing.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is zero-copy data sharing and how does it differ from exporting files?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Zero-copy sharing grants a consumer live, read-only access to the provider's data via metadata references, so the consumer queries the provider's single stored copy in place with their own compute -- no bytes are copied or transferred. File export instead physically copies data to the consumer, creating a stale duplicate that must be reconciled and re-shipped on every update. Sharing is always current, has no duplicate storage, and can be revoked instantly.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want the metadata-reference idea and the contrast with stale, duplicated file exports.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a data marketplace in the warehouse context?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A marketplace (Snowflake Marketplace, BigQuery Analytics Hub, AWS Data Exchange) is a catalog layered on the sharing primitive where providers publish listings -- free, public, or paid -- that consumers discover and subscribe to, instantly getting zero-copy access to the dataset. It turns data into a discoverable, monetizable product served to many consumers from one copy.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Connect it to sharing: the marketplace adds discovery, subscription, and billing on top of zero-copy access.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you share data safely without exposing PII?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Never share raw base tables. Build secure/authorized views that project only allowed columns (aggregating or de-identifying sensitive fields) and apply row-level policies so each consumer sees only its entitled rows. Add only those views to the share/listing/datashare. Because consumers query live, tightening a view or revoking the share takes effect immediately.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key is governance at the share boundary via secure views + row policies, not data movement.

intermediateQuestions.question: In standard data sharing, who pays for storage and who pays for compute?
intermediateQuestions.answer: The provider pays to store the data once; the consumer brings and pays for their own compute to query it. This clean split is why one provider can serve many consumers cheaply. The exception is a Snowflake reader account, used to serve a non-Snowflake consumer, where the provider pays for that consumer's query compute.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show you understand the economics that make marketplaces viable, plus the reader-account exception.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you serve a globally-distributed set of consumers from a single dataset, and what are the trade-offs?
advancedQuestions.answer: In-region sharing is instant metadata, but cross-region/cross-cloud requires replicating the dataset to each target region first, after which local consumers get zero-copy access. So you replicate the share per region: this gives every region low-latency local access but incurs duplicate storage and transfer cost and a replication lag, and each replica must be kept consistent and monitored. The alternative -- serving all regions from one region -- adds query latency/egress and is usually worse.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Strong answers state the replication requirement, the cost/lag trade-off, and that replicas double as DR copies.

advancedQuestions.question: What are the failure modes of a live data-sharing relationship and how do you prevent them?
advancedQuestions.answer: The main failure modes are: (1) PII/over-exposure from sharing raw tables -- prevented by secure/authorized views with column projection and row policies; (2) provider schema drift breaking consumer queries -- prevented by sharing stable, versioned views as the contract surface; (3) cross-region shares silently failing -- prevented by explicit replication and lag monitoring; and (4) compute-cost surprises -- prevented by pruning-friendly views, limits, and clarity on the provider/consumer pay model. Auditing grants and exposed objects catches accidental exposure.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the governance and operational failure modes and their concrete mitigations, showing sharing is a governance problem.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A partner asks for daily access to your order data, but you must not expose customer PII and must be able to cut access when the partnership ends. Design the share.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: This is a governance-at-the-boundary problem: expose only a de-identified, aggregated slice via a secure view, restrict rows to the partner's scope, share the view (not the table), and rely on instant revocation. Keep the view stable so your schema changes don't break them.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Create a secure view over the orders table that projects only non-PII columns (order date, region, product, quantity, amount) and applies a row policy limiting to the partner's scope. Create a share, grant USAGE on the db/schema and SELECT on the view only, and add the partner's account. They mount it read-only and query live data with their own compute daily. When the partnership ends, remove their account from the share -- access drops instantly with no orphaned copies. Version the view so base-table refactors don't break them.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a monetized data-product platform where your company sells governed, live datasets to thousands of global customers.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Build governed secure/authorized views over source data with per-customer row-level entitlements and full PII exclusion. Publish them as Marketplace/Analytics Hub listings (private offers for paid/commercial, public for samples). Onboard customers via subscription/grant (zero-copy, instant). Replicate the share to each region so global customers get local zero-copy access. Bill via the marketplace; customers query with their own compute. Manage all share/listing/policy definitions as IaC and audit every grant.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Consumer-pays economics make serving many customers cheap, but reader accounts (for non-platform customers) shift compute cost to you. Per-region replication gives low latency but duplicates storage and adds transfer cost and lag. Rich per-customer row entitlements add governance complexity but are essential for commercial isolation. Public listings maximize reach; private offers maximize control and pricing.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Serve unlimited consumers from one stored copy per region (metadata onboarding); replicate per region for global latency; template new listings and per-customer policies via IaC; monitor subscriptions, exposed objects, replication lag/cost, and consumer query patterns; and keep secure views stable and versioned so scaling the customer base never requires reworking consumer integrations.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Data sharing grants consumers live, read-only, zero-copy access to a provider's warehouse data queried in place with the consumer's own compute; a marketplace adds discovery, subscription, and monetization on top.
keyConcepts: Zero-copy: consumer queries provider's storage via metadata; no copy, always live, instant onboarding/revocation.
Compute split: provider stores once; consumer pays for its own queries (except Snowflake reader accounts).
Govern at the boundary: share secure/authorized views + row policies, never raw PII tables.
Primitives: Snowflake Share/Marketplace, BigQuery Analytics Hub listing/exchange, Redshift datashare/AWS Data Exchange.
Cross-region needs replication first; then local consumers get zero-copy access.
formulas: Provider cost = storage(1 copy) [+ replica storage/transfer per extra region] [+ reader-account compute].
Consumer cost = own query compute over shared data (bytes/slots/credits/RPUs).
Onboarding effort = O(1) metadata grant, independent of dataset size.
commands: Snowflake: CREATE SHARE s; GRANT SELECT ON VIEW v TO SHARE s; ALTER SHARE s ADD ACCOUNTS = CONSUMER_ACCT;
Snowflake (consumer): CREATE DATABASE d FROM SHARE PROVIDER_ACCT.s;
BigQuery: bq mk --data_exchange ex; bq mk --listing --data_exchange=ex --source_dataset=proj:ds listing1
Redshift: CREATE DATASHARE s; ALTER DATASHARE s ADD TABLE analytics.v; GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE s TO ACCOUNT '123456789012';
Redshift (consumer): CREATE DATABASE db FROM DATASHARE s OF NAMESPACE '<guid>';
interviewPoints: Zero-copy vs stale file exports; sharing is a governance problem, not data movement.
Consumer pays compute; provider stores once (reader accounts flip compute to provider).
Always share secure/authorized views with row policies, never raw PII.
Cross-region requires replication; replicas double as DR.
Access is instantly revocable with no orphaned copies.
quickNotes: Analytics Hub subscription creates a read-only linked dataset.
Snowflake Marketplace: public/free vs private/paid listings and offers.
Keep shared views stable and versioned so provider refactors don't break consumers.
Audit exposed objects (svv_datashare_objects / share metadata) regularly.

keyTakeaways: Zero-copy sharing grants consumers live, read-only access to the provider's single stored copy via metadata, eliminating inter-company ETL, duplicate storage, staleness, and slow onboarding.

The economics split cleanly: the provider stores data once and the consumer pays for its own query compute -- except Snowflake reader accounts, where the provider pays to serve non-customer consumers.
Sharing is fundamentally a governance problem: expose only secure/authorized views with column projection and per-consumer row policies, never raw PII tables, and audit every grant and listing.

Marketplaces (Snowflake Marketplace, BigQuery Analytics Hub, AWS Data Exchange) turn data into a discoverable, monetizable product served to many consumers from one copy, with instant subscription and revocation.
In-region sharing is instant metadata, but cross-region/cross-cloud sharing requires replicating the data to the target region first; those replicas also serve as disaster-recovery copies.
